name: Supply Chain Use Case
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Tracing a Mango in 2.2 Seconds, and Why the Shipping Industry Said No
lesson.summary: Two of the most famous blockchain pilots ever run, Walmart's food-traceability work with IBM and the Maersk-IBM shipping platform TradeLens, show both the real appeal and the real limits of blockchain in supply chains.
lesson.body:
Supply chains are a natural place to look for blockchain's promised benefits, because they genuinely involve the property the blockchain definition centers on: multiple independent organizations, farmers, processors, shippers, distributors, and retailers, that do not fully trust each other and do not share a common database today. When something goes wrong, like a food safety recall, tracing a product back through that chain by phone calls and paper records can take days. Walmart's food safety team, working with IBM, ran a now-famous demonstration of this problem: tracing a package of sliced mangoes back to the specific farm it came from took roughly six days using the company's existing paper-based systems. Using a blockchain-based system, built with IBM and later known as IBM Food Trust, the same trace took about two seconds. That gap, days versus seconds, is a genuinely compelling illustration of why a shared, tamper-evident record across many parties can beat a paper trail scattered across many separate filing cabinets.

Following that demonstration, Walmart required many of its leafy-green vegetable suppliers to join a blockchain-based traceability system by 2019, partly in response to E. coli outbreaks that had made fast tracing a food-safety priority. IBM Food Trust grew for a period around this case, but over the following years the standalone platform was scaled back and consolidated rather than expanding into the industry-wide standard some early coverage predicted. This is worth sitting with honestly rather than glossing over. The participants who most needed blockchain's specific properties, independent farms and distributors that did not want to hand control of the shared record to any single company among them, got real value from the system. But for many other participants, what they actually needed was simply reliable, fast, shared read access to a traceability log, and a well-designed permissioned database with an audit trail and an API can provide that without the overhead of running a distributed ledger.

The clearest cautionary tale in supply-chain blockchain is TradeLens, a platform built by Maersk, the world's largest container shipping company, together with IBM. The goal was ambitious: digitize the enormous paper trail behind global shipping, bills of lading, customs forms, and cargo documentation, onto a shared ledger that shipping lines, ports, customs authorities, and freight forwarders could all use. The technology largely worked. The business did not. Maersk's competitors, other major shipping lines, were reluctant to build critical parts of their operations on a platform that looked, structurally and reputationally, like Maersk's own infrastructure rather than neutral industry-wide infrastructure. Without broad participation from rival carriers, the platform's value as a shared record collapsed, since a traceability ledger is only useful if the parties you need to trace are actually on it. Maersk and IBM announced they were shutting TradeLens down in 2022, citing that it had not achieved the level of industry-wide collaboration needed to become commercially viable.

Applying the case-study-analysis checklist to both stories side by side is instructive. Both were technically functional pilots that scaled to real production use for a period. The difference was not cryptography, it was governance: Walmart had the market power to mandate supplier participation, while Maersk, despite its size, could not compel competitors to join a platform they perceived it as controlling. The honest overall verdict on supply-chain blockchain is that it remains one of the more defensible use cases in principle, because the underlying multi-party trust problem is real, but the track record so far is genuinely mixed. Some efforts, particularly narrower ones with a dominant party able to require participation, have persisted in some form; other, broader consortium efforts have been quietly wound down.
